newsitem.title: USA: FedEx cargo plane had other troubled landings.
newsitem.headline: FedEx cargo plane had other troubled landings.

text.p: The Federal Express plane that crashed Thursday sustained substantial damage in another hard landing and had two emergency landings in less than four years of commercial use, official records showed.
The MD11F cargo plane's most traumatic landing, until the crash at Newark International Airport, occurred Nov. 4, 1994, at Anchorage International Airport in Alaska.

A National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) report on the accident noted that on a day with little wind and good conditions the plane, commissioned in 1993, landed hard, bounced and the aft fuselage was damaged after the tail hit the runway. During repairs maintenance workers found that the aft skin of the plane had been scraped off.

A hard landing occurs when a plane exceeds the specified normal landing requirements, such as too high a speed or it is overweight or it bounces or hits too hard and the crew suspects there may be damage from the landing.

The NTSB said the 1994 accident was caused by "the crew's improper recovery from a bounced landing" and that factors associated with the accident included crew members' "lack of familiarity with the airplane, their inadequate control of the aircraft and the captain's delayed remedial action."
Proper repairs were done on the aircraft after the accident.
In October 1993 the MD11F was forced to make an emergency landing after the crew discovered that one of its engines was loose. The pilot shut down the engine and dumped 90,000 pounds of fuel.

Maintenance workers discovered an oil leak and a loose connector on a fuel discharge line. The line was tightened, the oil serviced and the engine appeared to be running well afterwards, official reports show.
Another emergency landing occurred in January 1995 when a left wing flap malfunctioned. Official reports showed that it was a false warning while the plane was climbing.
Five people miraculously walked away almost unscathed after the plane crash-landed Thursday, overturned and burst into flames.
NTSB investigator John Goglia told reporters at New Jersey's Newark Airport that one of the flight recorders had been found, but not yet removed from the plane.
"It appears to me to be a fuel fire, there's many thousands of gallons on an airplane even at the end of its trip and there is a strong smell of kerosene all over the place," Goglia said.
The cause of the crash, which happened at 1:35 a.m. EDT (0535 GMT), could not be immediately known, Goglia said.
